rows.description: A wise decider asks what she would judge if she had never seen the first figure, then gathers two or three independent comparisons before deciding.

rows.description: After hearing one scary story about a dog bite, a child decides all dogs are dangerous. The most memorable case feels like the most common one.

rows.description: A teenager who keeps seeing viral accident clips believes travel or the city is far riskier than it is. Frequency of exposure is mistaken for frequency in real life.

rows.description: A student fears flying or a rare illness after dramatic coverage but rides a scooter without a helmet. Memorable dangers crowd out common ones.

rows.description: A new parent sees relatives panic over a kidnapping rumour forwarded on WhatsApp while ignoring the everyday risks at home. He asks what the actual numbers say.

rows.description: A mature person pauses when a story feels vivid, asks how often it truly happens, and looks up reliable figures before changing her habits or fears.

rows.description: A child assumes the quiet boy with glasses must be the topper and the loud boy must be weak. Appearance stands in for real evidence about ability.

rows.description: A teenager decides who is good at maths, sports or trouble from how someone looks or speaks, and is surprised when reality disagrees. The match to a type feels like proof.

rows.description: A student assumes a confident, fluent speaker will run a good project and overlooks a quieter but more reliable teammate. Style is mistaken for competence.
